evidence.text: The received text gives “此字本闕” (“this entry was originally missing”). Its appended note says Sun Mian’s Tangyun quote gives a form from 竹 and 犬 meaning “喜也”; Li Yangbing’s recension instead uses 竹 and 夭 and offers the explanation that wind-bent bamboo resembles a person laughing. The note itself questions Li’s explanation.

evidence.field: 說文解字 and 說文解字注 entries; script forms; cited uses
evidence.text: The page reproduces the received Shuowen note and a longer Duan Yucai commentary. That commentary describes competing transmitted forms and editorial changes, including 竹+犬 and 竹+夭, but is a later textual analysis, not direct proof of the graph’s origin. The page indexes Chu manuscript and Han slips as examples; its cited classical uses include 《詩·邶風·終風》“顧我則笑” and 《論語·憲問》“樂然後笑”. It also records later senses including ridicule, joking, and metaphorical flower-opening; these glosses do not alone establish the chronology or semantic path of those extensions.

evidence.field: 字源; graph forms and analyses
evidence.text: The entry reports that excavated Warring States through Han manuscript forms are written with components interpreted as 艸 and 犬, contrasting these with received dictionary forms in the 竹 section and forms analyzed as 竹+犬 or 竹+夭. It presents a proposed history in which 艸 was confused with 竹 and 犬 with 夭, and also lists alternative proposals involving 芺 or a pictorial form. These are competing hypotheses summarized by the entry, not settled conclusions. It reports a Zhengzhang series assigning 笑 *sqʰows and 夭 *qoːwʔ, *qrow, *qrowʔ, and a separate Baxter–Sagart row for 笑.

gaps: No primary artifact catalog or inspected manuscript image was obtained to verify the reported Warring States and Han graph shapes, their exact loci, or dating; no glyph image was visually inspected.

The first physical attestation of 笑 and the exact semantic contexts of the earliest manuscript examples remain unverified. Classical-text quotations attest lexical usage in received texts, not dated physical graphs.

The initial 艸+犬 interpretation is disputed: evidence retrieved does not establish whether 艸 was phonetic, semantic, or a graphic predecessor, nor whether 犬 was semantic or part of a corrupted/pictorial shape. The proposed 竹+夭 phonetic analysis likewise lacks independent sound-history evidence beyond reconstructed readings and transmitted attribution.
The potential graph corruption or substitution sequence among 艸/竹 and 犬/夭 is not settled; the proposed 芺 intermediary and pictorial “smiling face” accounts remain unsupported here by primary sources.
The origin and chronology of later senses (ridicule, joke, flower-opening, and honorific “please accept”) were not established; dictionary gloss order is not a chronology.

Local reading rows checked: sources/unihan/Unihan_Readings.txt gives kMandarin xiào for 咲 and 笑; sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv gives 笑 MC sjewH, OC *[s-l]aw-s, gloss “to laugh”. These are local data checks, not external citations. Official U+7B11 record verified. U+54B2 official Unihan page could not be accessed despite repeated attempts, so its required official click-through citation is unavailable.

The component 夭’s current and historical readings were not checked against local rows or an official Unihan record; Zhengzhang reconstructions on the opened page are secondary-source assertions. Thus a sound-array entry for 夭 is not independently complete.
No explicit phonetic-loan analysis is established for this character; the loan-specific object/name issue therefore does not apply.

The exact earliest physical graph attestation, artifact locus, archaeological dating and form remain unverified. A CUHK dictionary page reports a Mawangdui manuscript use at line 152, while a secondary report dates the manuscript context to early Western Han; the manuscript’s actual graph image and line were not inspected.

The earliest 艸+犬 graph’s component roles remain unsettled. Retrieved sources disagree or list alternatives; no primary paleographic study was inspected to establish whether 艸 was phonetic, semantic, or a graphic predecessor, or whether 犬 later became 夭 through corruption.

No independent evidence establishes that 夭’s pronunciation was historically close enough to 笑 to serve as its phonetic in the received form. The stated Zhengzhang readings are secondary-source transcriptions. Local Baxter–Sagart input has a 笑 row only, not a 夭 row, and therefore does not establish a same-system comparison.
The official Unihan pages for 笑, 夭, and 艸 returned internal errors; only 笑’s local kMandarin row was supplied. No current Unihan component readings are claimed.

No inspected dated physical graph image was found for selection. The available seal-script file is a modern redraw of a received Shuowen-style form and must not be represented as an artifact. The linked Xiaoxuetang page was checked for its label, but a reusable direct image URL and applicable rights notice were not verified in this run.
